---
title: "4B. Community differences (track B: marine plankton)"
format:
  html:
    toc: false
---

*Analyse differences in community composition between samples — beta diversity — using Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA).*

### Calculate Bray-Curtis dissimilarity

Bray-Curtis dissimilarity compares the abundances of taxa in two samples, from 0 for identical communities to 1 for communities with nothing in common. Both datasets use the same primers, so we can compare them at ASV level.

We give the columns the names that [`ecolongr`](https://github.com/biodiversitydata-se/ecolongr){target="_blank"} expects by default, turn the counts into relative abundances so that sequencing depth does not affect the comparison, and calculate the dissimilarities:

```r
asv_counts <- merged$counts |>
  transmute(sample = eventID, taxon = taxonID, quant = organismQuantity)

bray <- asv_counts |>
  el_decostand("total") |>
  el_vegdist("bray", samples = events$eventID)
```

`el_decostand()` and `el_vegdist()` work like `decostand()` and `vegdist()` in the `vegan` package, but on the long table, without reading it into R. `samples =` makes the result follow the order of the rows in `events`, which we rely on when plotting. The result is an ordinary `dist` object that `vegan` and base R can use.

### Run PCoA

Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) represents the dissimilarities among samples in a smaller number of dimensions:

```r
pcoa <- cmdscale(bray, k = 2, eig = TRUE)

# Share of the positive eigenvalues held by each of the first two axes
axis_share <- pcoa$eig[1:2] / sum(pcoa$eig[pcoa$eig > 0])
round(100 * axis_share, 1)
```

### Plot PCoA results

We plot the PCoA once per dataset, with all samples in grey in the background. Colour shows the day of year and size the salinity, as on the maps:

```r
plot_pcoa <- function() {
  xlab <- paste0("PC1 (", round(100 * axis_share[1]), "%)")
  ylab <- paste0("PC2 (", round(100 * axis_share[2]), "%)")
  x <- pcoa$points[, 1]
  y <- pcoa$points[, 2]

  layout(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE), heights = c(4, 1))
  par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))

  for (dataset in c("2019-2020", "2013")) {
    ix <- events$dataset == dataset
    plot(x, y, col = "grey85", pch = 16, cex = 0.8,
         xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = dataset)
    points(x[ix], y[ix], pch = dataset_pch[dataset], col = "black",
           bg = color_yday[events$yday[ix]], cex = point_size(events$salinity[ix], 0.8, 15))
  }

  par(mar = c(3, 2, 1, 2))
  plot(1:366, rep(1, 366), col = color_yday, pch = "|", cex = 3,
       axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", ylim = c(0.9, 1.3))
  axis(1, at = c(1, 182, 366))
  text(183, 1.2, "Day of year")

  plot(c(2, 18, 34), rep(1, 3), pch = 1, cex = 0.8 + c(2, 18, 34) / 15,
       xlim = c(-5, 40), ylim = c(0.9, 1.3), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  axis(1, at = c(2, 18, 34))
  text(18, 1.2, "Salinity")
}

plot_pcoa()
```

The first axis explains about a third of the variation and follows salinity: the samples from the brackish Baltic Sea are on the left, and those from the saltier Kattegat and Skagerrak on the right. Within each group, the second axis follows the season. The samples from the 2013 transect fall in the same pattern as the later ones, which suggests that the two datasets can be compared.
